rv.q: My quibbles are nothing more than that: I’d gladly see “Flying Over Sunset” again right away.
It's a valiant and intriguing journey into uncharted territory.
Overlong and occasionally (but only occasionally) a bit tedious, the last third of the show loses its way.
That’s all cool, but it cannot solve that central issue of the lack of dramatic tension nor the overly languid nature of this production.
This, alas, is not musical theater on acid; this is acid on musical theater.
Though sometimes mesmerizing, “Flying Over Sunset,” the new musical about LSD that opened there on Monday, is mostly bewildering, and further proof that transcendence can’t be shared.
Beyond oddness, though, “Flying Over Sunset” is unforgivably dull onstage.
The musical feels overstuffed and underdeveloped, with three fascinating subjects that never quite gel into a cohesive theatrical experience despite the best efforts of a talented cast.
With that cautionary premise in mind, the creatives of this delectable theatrical bonbon treat us to a tasteful trip on the mild side.
The Vivian Beaumont is a big house to sign over to a musical so dramaturgically inept, so lacking in connection, philosophy, or fire.
That’s sort of what you experience with “Flying Over Sunset.”

If Flying Over Sunset doesn’t truly take us into the minds or souls of its distinguished subjects, it will likely make you more curious about them—and make you wish that getting high could be more of a spectator sport.
But an abundance of interesting ideas never coalesces into the hallucinatory, revelatory experience the show seems to promise.
More problematic, the three main characters, who are self-absorbed to begin with, turn even more inward when stoned, putting the brakes on any kind of dramatic or comedic tension between them.
I was never completely persuaded that these three famous figures belong in the same musical.
Director Lapine proves too indulgent of Lapine the librettist, allowing the proceedings to ramble on to the point of tedium.

But alas, the startling contradictions and dazzling talents that made legends out of Huxley, Luce, and Grant are left unexplored by Lapine’s thudding book, and are rendered tediously monotone in Kitt and Korie’s score, which neither mirrors nor rebels against its time period’s soundscapes.
It’s not that these aren’t real issues, but Lapine’s script feels a bit Wikipedia-like, which is one reason why the tedium starts to set in long before the final curtain.
But something vital is missing—an emotional center, a reason to care whether or not this diverse trio will take the drug and about what they discover on their trip.
Instead, it just bears out the truth that there’s no worse trip than having to witness somebody else’s.

Perhaps too much is promised in the beginning: Three icons from the 1950s are introduced on stage, one by one, and they have almost nothing in common with each other — except for the fact that Cary Grant, Clare Boothe Luce and Aldous Huxley all do LSD, which back then was not illegal.
The excellent cast does what it can with the skimpy and emaciated story but cannot save it from seeming like a missed opportunity and a big disappointment considering the talent involved.
This show has a lot of wheel-spinning and minimal rewards.
“Flying Over Sunset” is an artistic misfire – and a nearly three-hour slog to sit through.
The trippy spectacle of an LSD-high Grant singing, "I am a giant penis rocket ship! Zoom! Kaboom!" — yes, really — can't keep this from being a trek to nowhere.
“Till the funny money rolls right in” to an old music hall tune is a show stopper.
For a script that takes such a fantastic leap of imagination, Flying Over Sunset, unfortunately, recoils back into the safety of clichés before it can start spreading its wings of fantasy.

But this is one rambling, pointless head-scratcher of a show, not redeemed by the charm of its cast or the random bit of camp eccentricity, such as Yazbeck’s Grant whooshing around the stage declaring, “I am a giant penis rocket ship!”

cn.t: Critics find this LSD-themed musical about Cary Grant, Aldous Huxley, and Clare Boothe Luce visually stunning but dramatically inert, with most comparing it to watching other people's boring trips. Yazbeck's tap dancing stands out in an otherwise dull experience.

sg.ra: Thrust stage projects into the audience here, so front-center puts you directly in the actors' playing space with 180-degree eye contact. However, SeatPlan and JK's TheatreScene both warn the thrust's elevated downstage lip can obscure upstage action, and the shallow rake this close means you look up at performers working the far edge of the thrust.

At the middle of the thrust's semicircle, the stadium-style rake lifts you over heads in front while the curved row geometry keeps you square to the playing area — the thrust no longer feels side-on because you're on its central axis. SeatPlan, Headout, TickPick and Broadway Scene all converge on D-K center as the best sightlines in the house.

Sits on the central axis of the thrust so you see the three-sided staging in balance rather than from an angle. LCT's official chart confirms Row P has a dedicated step-up giving it elevation above Row O, and Headout lists L, P, O, K as the value-balance rows. At a thrust stage, back-center beats side-front because you read the full geometry of audience-wrapping blocking.

On a thrust stage, the far-side Orchestra seats end up looking ACROSS the playing space rather than at it — you see actors' profiles and often stare at the back of the thrust's far edge. SeatPlan: 'restricted views depending on staging.' JK's TheatreScene explicitly warns 'avoid the 4 or 5 seats closest to the wall.' BWW Forum thread 1082386 exists specifically because patrons worry about side-seat restriction at this venue.

The elevated Loge wraps the same semicircle as the Orchestra but 2 flights up (LCT: 30 steps), giving you the map-view of the thrust's three-sided blocking that's impossible from Orchestra. TickPick: 'Center, in the first three rows' is premium. SeatPlan confirms 'no bar or obstructions' at the front edge. For a thrust stage this is arguably a better seat than Orchestra for geometry-heavy stagings.

Only 5 rows exist in the Loge, so 'back Loge' is still close. TickPick: 'Rows D and E of Center Left and Center Right offer amazing views at a lower cost.' JK's TheatreScene paid $99 for similar seats and called them 'budget-friendly and worth every penny... view not appreciably different than the first few rows.' Elevated angle reads the thrust's three-sided blocking well even from slight side.

Compounds both weaknesses of a thrust-stage venue: you're on the far side of the semicircle AND at the back of the elevated tier, so the upstage portion of the thrust turns away from you. TickPick names Loge R Row E Seat 509 as the worked example: 'the rear end of the stage is going to be obstructed.' SeatPlan: 'Views from the Loge can feel distant, especially at the far sides.'
